title: Structural, Physiological and Behavioural Adaptations
subtitle: Three kinds of survival feature
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: Use plant and animal examples to explain how structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations shaped by evolution enable survival in their environment
inquiryQuestion: How do adaptations shaped by evolution enable survival?
lessonIntent: Students can classify adaptations as structural, physiological or behavioural and explain, with plant and animal examples, how each enables survival.
examSkill: Link every adaptation: feature → how it works → survival in a named environment, and trace it back to selection on inherited variation.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome to HSC Science. This is Biology. Today, the three kinds of adaptation. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Three kinds of trick
scenes.body: A red kangaroo licks its forearms to cool down, makes extra-concentrated urine to save water, and rests in shade through the heat of the day.
scenes.callout: Can you name what type each one is?
scenes.caption: Survival features come in three kinds: structural, physiological and behavioural.

voiceover.text: Arid Australia is tough on animals, from the thorny devil to the red kangaroo. A red kangaroo survives it with a whole kit of tricks. It rests in shade through the heat of the day. It makes extra-concentrated urine to save water. And it has a fine network of blood vessels in its forearms, where it can cool its blood. Three completely different kinds of survival trick. One is about what the body is built like, one is about what goes on inside, and one is about what the animal does. Can you name each type?

scenes.heading: Three types of adaptation
scenes.body: Structural: a body part you could draw. Physiological: an internal process. Behavioural: an action the organism performs.

bullets.text: Structural: cactus spines, thick polar bear fur.
Physiological: mangrove salt glands, hopping mouse urine.
Behavioural: kangaroo resting in shade, sunflowers tracking the sun.

scenes.callout: Can you draw it? Is it a process? Is it an action?
scenes.caption: Plant and animal examples of structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations.

voiceover.text: Adaptations come in three types. A structural adaptation is a physical feature of the body, its shape, size, covering or parts. The test is simple. If you can see it or draw it, it's structural. A cactus has spines, which are reduced leaves that cut water loss. A polar bear has thick insulating fur. A physiological adaptation is an internal process, usually chemical or metabolic. A grey mangrove excretes excess salt through glands on its leaves. The spinifex hopping mouse makes some of the most concentrated urine of any mammal. A behavioural adaptation is an inherited action. A red kangaroo rests in shade through the midday heat, and young sunflowers turn to track the sun.

scenes.heading: All three at once
scenes.body: The red kangaroo shows structural, physiological and behavioural adaptations working as one system.

bullets.text: Structural: large ears, forearm blood vessels.
Behavioural: rests in shade, licks its forearms.

scenes.caption: Red kangaroo: ears and forearm vessels, concentrated urine, shade and forearm licking.

voiceover.text: One organism usually has all three types working together. Take the red kangaroo in arid Australia. Structurally, it has large ears that lose heat, and a network of blood vessels just under the skin of its forearms. Physiologically, its kidneys produce highly concentrated urine, so it excretes waste in very little water. Behaviourally, it rests in shade through the hottest part of the day and feeds around dawn and dusk. And it licks saliva onto its forearms, so evaporation cools the blood in that network. Notice how they interlock. The licking is a behaviour, but it only works because of the structural blood vessels, and it spends water the kidneys have saved.

scenes.heading: Shaped by evolution
scenes.body: Every adaptation traces back to inherited variation and a selective pressure.

bullets.text: Those with the helpful feature survive and reproduce more.
Over generations the feature becomes common.

scenes.callout: Feature → how it works → survival in that environment.
scenes.caption: Adaptations arise by natural selection; explain the survival link.

voiceover.text: Where do adaptations come from? Not from an individual trying. Within any population, individuals vary. When a selective pressure acts, like heat, drought or predators, the individuals whose inherited features best fit the environment survive and reproduce more, and pass those features on. Over many generations, the helpful feature becomes common. That's the adaptation. So a top answer never just names a feature. It links the feature, to how it works, to survival in that environment. Not, the cactus has spines. But, the cactus's spines are reduced leaves with very little surface area, which cuts water loss in a hot, dry place, so individuals with them survived drought and the feature spread.

footer.text: Answer shape: feature → how it works → survival

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Adaptation: an inherited feature, shaped by natural selection, that increases survival and reproduction.
Structural adaptation: a physical feature of the body.
Physiological adaptation: an internal chemical or metabolic process.
Behavioural adaptation: an inherited action or behaviour.
Selective pressure: an environmental factor that favours some variants.

scenes.caption: Adaptation, structural, physiological, behavioural, selective pressure.

voiceover.text: Five terms. An adaptation is an inherited feature, shaped by natural selection, that increases an organism's chance of surviving and reproducing in its environment. A structural adaptation is a physical feature of the body, like thick fur or long roots. A physiological adaptation is an internal, often chemical or metabolic, process, like concentrated urine or venom. A behavioural adaptation is an inherited action, like migrating or being active at night. And a selective pressure is an environmental factor, like heat, drought or predators, that favours some variants over others.

scenes.heading: Sort and explain
scenes.question: Classify each and explain how it helps survival: (a) a cactus’s thick waxy cuticle; (b) a desert frog burrowing and staying dormant in drought; (c) a eucalypt producing oils that deter herbivores.
scenes.coachNote: Every line needs "so that" or "which means", then a survival consequence.
steps: (a) Structural: the waxy layer waterproofs the leaf surface, so less water is lost in hot, dry conditions.
(b) Behavioural: burrowing and dormancy mean the frog avoids heat and drying out until rain returns.
(c) Physiological: producing oils is an internal chemical process, so fewer leaves are eaten.
Answer: structural, behavioural, physiological, each linked to survival in its environment.
scenes.caption: Cuticle is structural, burrowing is behavioural, oil production is physiological.

voiceover.text: Let's sort and explain three features. The rule is that every answer needs a consequence, so that, or which means, then survival. A, a cactus's thick waxy cuticle. That's structural, a body part. The wax waterproofs the surface, so less water is lost in hot, dry conditions. B, a desert frog burrows underground and stays dormant in drought. That's behavioural, something it does, which means it avoids heat and drying out until rain returns. C, a eucalypt makes oils that deter herbivores. That's physiological, an internal chemical process, so fewer of its leaves are eaten.

scenes.heading: Growing what you need
scenes.body: Wrong: an organism develops an adaptation during its lifetime because it needs one.
scenes.secondary: Right: adaptations are inherited features that already vary in a population. Natural selection favours the individuals that happen to carry the helpful variant, so it becomes more common over generations.
scenes.callout: No individual grows an adaptation because it is useful.
scenes.caption: Adaptations are inherited and spread by selection; they are not grown on demand.

voiceover.text: Here's the misconception to fix. Students write that an organism develops an adaptation during its lifetime, because it needs one. That's wrong. Adaptations are inherited features that already vary within a population. Natural selection favours the individuals that happen to carry the helpful variant, so over generations the adaptation becomes more common. A cactus didn't grow spines because it was thirsty, and a kangaroo didn't choose efficient kidneys. Individuals with those features survived and reproduced more, and passed them on.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A plant closes its stomata in the heat of the day. Is this structural, physiological or behavioural?
scenes.pausePrompt: Pause: is there a part, a process, and an action here?
answerSteps: The stoma itself is a structure.
Closing is driven by guard-cell turgor changes: a physiological process.
The timing, closing in the heat of the day, has the character of a behaviour.
Answer: it spans all three. Say so, then justify the category you choose.
scenes.caption: Stomatal closing spans all three categories; justify your choice.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A plant closes its stomata in the heat of the day. Is that structural, physiological or behavioural? Pause, and look for a part, a process and an action. Here's the answer. The stoma itself is a structure. The closing is driven by changes in the guard cells' turgor, a physiological process. And the timing, closing in the heat of the day, has the character of a behaviour. So it genuinely spans all three. That's fine. The categories are levels of description. Say that it overlaps, then justify the category you choose.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Structural: a body part you could draw.
Physiological: an internal chemical or metabolic process.
One organism usually has all three working together.
Adaptations arise by selection on inherited variation.
scenes.finalPrompt: Name the type, then feature → how it works → survival in that environment.
scenes.caption: Three types of adaptation, all shaped by natural selection.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. A structural adaptation is a body part you could draw. A physiological adaptation is an internal process. A behavioural adaptation is an inherited action. One organism, like the red kangaroo, usually has all three working together. And every adaptation arises by natural selection on inherited variation. Next lesson, we'll measure structural adaptations for water balance in Australian plants.
